headline: Fort Trumbull Rip Still Turning: Bluefish Committed, Bass Staging Deep
subhead: The seam off the fort is holding bait and blues on every ebb, while the striper bite waits on the bunker to bunch up.
body_markdown:
The current off Fort Trumbull has been running hard and clean on the back half of the ebb all week, and that seam where the river water pours past the old fort wall into the harbor channel has been the most consistent read on this stretch of the Thames. Water off New London has been sitting in the high 60s, closer to 69 degrees, and that's warm enough to keep bait tight to structure rather than scattered across open water. That's the pattern that's been setting up for ten days now — bluefish committed and predictable, striped bass present but not yet organized into the kind of push that makes September memorable on this river.

We flagged this last week — said to expect stability through the short-term window with no major changes in this sheltered zone — and that's exactly what's played out. No fronts have come through to stir things up, the harbor has stayed clean, and the bite has held its shape day to day rather than swinging hot and cold. That kind of steadiness is a gift this time of year, because it means anglers can plan around known windows instead of chasing a moving target.

Bluefish are the dependable half of that equation right now, and they've been tracking bunker density just like we said they would. Peanut and adult bunker have been pushing through the Gold Star Bridge pilings on the last two hours of the ebb, and the blues have been parked underneath, working the pilings like a feeding station. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, dropped tight to the concrete and swept with the current, have been drawing consistent strikes from blues in the 3 to 6-pound class. Chunk bunker fished on a fish-finder rig off the Fort Trumbull rocks has also been producing, particularly in the last hour of daylight when the current is still moving but the sun's off the water. Topwater has had its moments too — poppers worked off the rocks at Ocean Beach and Pleasure Beach during the early morning slack have drawn some violent surface strikes when bait is visibly nervous on top.

Striped bass are the harder read. They're in the system — boats working the deeper current seams below the Gold Star Bridge and in the mouth of the harbor near the state pier have picked bass in the 24 to 30-inch range on the last two hours of the incoming, mostly on eels drifted along bottom structure or bunker chunks fished tight to the channel edge. But it's not a blitz pattern yet, and anyone expecting surface commotion is going to be disappointed. These fish are holding deep, tucked against current breaks and rock piles rather than chasing bait on top, which tracks with what the moon is doing right now. We're building toward full, and that means tidal flow is only going to get stronger over the next several days, which should start concentrating bait harder in the same zones where bluefish are already parked. When that bait finally bunches up tight enough, the bass tend to commit fast — that's the pattern up and down this whole stretch of coast right now, and there's no reason the Thames should be any different once it happens.

Porgies have stayed a reliable side dish for anyone fishing bottom rigs off Groton, particularly around the drop-offs near the state pier and the deeper stretches toward Sarah's Ledge, where sandworms and clam strips on a simple hi-lo rig have kept rods bent for anyone willing to sit on anchor through a tide change. Blackfish are starting to show a little more interest around the rock piles and jetty structure near Avery Point and the mouth of Fishers Island Sound, though it's still early-season picking rather than a full-blown tautog bite — green crabs on a jig head, worked slow along the rocks on the bottom of the tide, have taken a few fish in the 14 to 18-inch range.

One thing worth watching given how close this harbor sits to Fishers Island Sound: bonito have been showing signs of pushing west out of Rhode Island waters, and if that spillover reaches the Race or the eastern Sound approaches, this river mouth and the water off Ocean Beach would be a logical place for them to show up next. Nothing confirmed yet on this side of the line, but it's worth keeping a small metal or epoxy jig rigged on light tackle in the boat just in case that shows up over the holiday weekend.

Looking at the next several days, expect the bluefish pattern to hold — warm water, strong current, bait tight to structure, and blues willing to eat anything that swims through the seam. The striper situation is the one to watch closely as the moon builds toward full over Labor Day weekend; if the bunker schools in the harbor and river mouth tighten up the way they have elsewhere on the coast, the bass bite here could shift from a deep, patient game to something a lot more aggressive in a short window. Until that happens, the smart play is working the known current breaks — Fort Trumbull on the ebb, the bridge pilings on the last of the tide — rather than searching for fish that haven't organized yet.
